introduction.heading: Why Draw It First?
introduction.description: Before you write a single class or CREATE TABLE, it pays to sketch the shape of the problem. A class diagram is a picture of your object model - which types exist, what data they hold, and how they're connected. An ER (entity-relationship) diagram is the same idea aimed at the database - which tables exist, their columns, and the keys that link them. The two are close cousins: most classes become tables, most fields become columns, and every "has a" line between classes becomes a foreign key or a join table. Getting the relationships and their multiplicity right on paper is far cheaper than discovering, three weeks into the course project, that an Order can only ever have one line item because you modeled it that way without noticing.

concepts.title: Class Box
concepts.description: A class is drawn as a three-part box: the name, then its attributes (fields), then its operations (methods). A leading - means private, + means public, # protected

concepts.title: Association, Aggregation, Composition
concepts.description: All three are "has a" links. A plain association is just "knows about"; aggregation (hollow diamond) is a whole-part where the part can outlive the whole; composition (filled diamond) is a whole-part where the part dies with the whole

concepts.title: Inheritance & Dependency
concepts.description: Inheritance (hollow triangle, "is a") means one class extends another; a dependency (dashed arrow, "uses") is a passing reference - a parameter or local variable - not a stored field

concepts.title: Multiplicity / Cardinality
concepts.description: The numbers at each end of a line - 1, 0..1, 1..*, * - say how many objects on this side relate to one object on the other. In ER terms this is one-to-one, one-to-many, or many-to-many

concepts.title: Entity, Attribute, Primary & Foreign Key
concepts.description: An ER entity is a table; attributes are columns; the primary key uniquely identifies a row; a foreign key is a column holding another table's primary key, which is how rows in different tables are linked

concepts.title: Normalization (1NF - 3NF)
concepts.description: A disciplined way of splitting tables so each fact is stored once: 1NF removes repeating groups, 2NF removes fields that depend on only part of a composite key, 3NF removes fields that depend on another non-key field

mapping.heading: From a Class Diagram to Tables
mapping.description: Turning an object model into a relational schema is mostly mechanical once you know the rules. A class becomes a table. A single-valued field becomes a column. A one-to-many association puts a foreign key on the 'many' side. A many-to-many association becomes its own join table with a foreign key to each side. Inheritance has a few options, but the simplest is one table per concrete class. Pick a domain below and watch the class diagram become CREATE TABLE statements.

gettingStarted.heading: Getting Started
steps: List the nouns in the problem statement - most become classes/entities, and the verbs between them hint at the relationships
For each class, write only the attributes you actually need; give every entity a primary key (an id column is the safe default)
Draw the line between two related classes and immediately label both ends with a multiplicity - don't leave an end blank
Decide whether a whole-part link is aggregation or composition by asking: if the whole is deleted, should the part be deleted too?
Convert one-to-many by putting a foreign key on the 'many' side; convert many-to-many by creating a join table with two foreign keys
Check each table against 3NF: does every non-key column depend on the whole key and nothing but the key?
Use a tool (draw.io, dbdiagram.io, or Mermaid) so the diagram stays editable - you will change it as the design settles

practiceTopics.title: The Four Relationship Types
practiceTopics.description: Switch between association, aggregation, composition, and inheritance and see the notation, a real code example, and whether the part can outlive the whole

practiceTopics.title: Cardinality & How It Maps to Keys
practiceTopics.description: Set the multiplicity on each end of a relationship and see the crow's-foot notation plus whether it becomes a foreign key or a join table

practiceTopics.title: Normalizing a Table to 3NF
practiceTopics.description: Take one messy table with repeating groups and partial dependencies and step it through 1NF, 2NF, and 3NF

fullExample.heading: Full Example, Step by Step
fullExample.title: Model a small library: class diagram, ER diagram, and the SQL schema
fullExample.description: A worked model of a lending library - members borrow book copies, books have authors - shown three ways: as a UML class model, as an ER diagram, and as the CREATE TABLE statements they translate into. Click through the steps to see how each relationship crosses from one representation to the next.

steps.label: The classes and their attributes
steps.explanation: Five classes. Book is the abstract title ('Clean Code'); BookCopy is a physical copy on a shelf with its own barcode. Splitting them is the single most common modeling fix - a library owns many copies of one book. Loan gets its own class because it carries dates that belong to neither a Member nor a BookCopy alone.

steps.label: A one-to-many: Book to BookCopy
steps.explanation: One Book has 1..* BookCopy, and each BookCopy belongs to exactly one Book. This is composition - a copy has no meaning without its book - so in SQL the copy table carries a NOT NULL foreign key back to book.

steps.label: A many-to-many: Book to Author
steps.explanation: A book can have several authors and an author writes many books, so neither side can hold a single foreign key. It becomes the book_author join table, whose primary key is the pair (book_id, author_id).

steps.label: A one-to-many with history: Member to Loan
steps.explanation: A Member has many Loans; each Loan points at one Member and one BookCopy and records the dates. Loan is an entity in its own right precisely because it holds attributes (borrowed_on, due_on, returned_on) that belong to the relationship, not to either end.

steps.label: The ER diagram: the same model as tables
steps.explanation: Every class became a table, every attribute a column, and the crow's-foot marks (the fork = 'many', the bar = 'one') restate the multiplicities. book_author is the only table with no surrogate id - its identity is the two foreign keys together.

steps.label: SQL: the composition becomes ON DELETE CASCADE
steps.explanation: book_copy holds a NOT NULL foreign key to book, so no copy can exist without a book. ON DELETE CASCADE is the direct translation of the filled diamond: remove the book row and the database removes its copies for you.

steps.label: SQL: the join table and the loan table
steps.explanation: book_author has no id of its own - PRIMARY KEY (book_id, author_id) makes the pair unique, so the same author can't be attached to the same book twice. loan became a full table because it carries its own columns (borrowed_on, due_on, returned_on) on top of the two foreign keys.

quiz.question: You delete an Invoice and its InvoiceLine rows should be deleted with it. Which relationship did you model?
quiz.explanation: Composition is a whole-part where the part cannot exist without the whole - deleting the whole deletes the parts. Aggregation would let the lines survive on their own.

quiz.question: A Student can enroll in many Courses and a Course has many Students. How is this stored relationally?
options: A foreign key on the student table
A foreign key on the course table
A join table with a foreign key to student and one to course
It can't be represented in SQL
quiz.explanation: A many-to-many needs a third table (enrollment) holding one foreign key to each side. A single foreign key on either table could only express one-to-many.

quiz.question: In the class box notation, what does a leading '-' before an attribute name mean?
quiz.explanation: '-' is private, '+' is public, '#' is protected. It has nothing to do with keys or persistence - that's the ER diagram's job.

quiz.question: A table has columns (order_id, product_id, quantity, product_name). The key is (order_id, product_id). Which normal form does it violate?
options: 2NF, because product_name depends on only part of the key
quiz.explanation: product_name depends on product_id alone, which is only part of the composite key - that's a partial dependency, the exact thing 2NF forbids. Move product_name to the product table.

quiz.question: Which link would you draw as a dependency (dashed arrow) rather than an association?
options: A method takes a PricingService parameter and uses it, but never stores it
quiz.explanation: A dependency is a transient 'uses' - a parameter or local variable. A stored field is an association; extends is inheritance.
